fields.sample_size: 52 individuals interviewed during 33 days of fieldwork in 2019 across north, central and southern Malawi (15 public officials, 1 intergovernmental organisation, 8 NGOs, 6 scientists/students, 22 general public from Lilongwe and eight study communities; 27 women and 25 men), with observations, workshops and secondary documents
fields.effect_estimate: National WaSH progress is real but statistics-driven management 'romanticises momentary achievement': under-capacity in shaping cultural practices, sustaining and maintaining infrastructure, and inequalities affecting those unable to pay; governance frameworks and compliance regimes are confounded by management toward statistical summaries so a large share of the population remains without basic drinking water or improved sanitation. Of the 22 public respondents only 4 (18.2%) had higher education. Qualitative and descriptive.
fields.study_design: qualitative case study (52 interviews, observation, workshops, secondary documents; one country)
fields.section: Full text: Research methods (52 respondents by category and gender); findings; Conclusion and policy priorities
fields.exact_location: Research methods (52 respondents by category and gender); findings; Conclusion and policy priorities

evidence_level: Single-study evidence: 52 interviews and fieldwork in Malawi (2019) on WaSH sector governance, read in full text 2026-10-04. Statistical summaries mask sustainability and equity gaps; governance frameworks and compliance regimes do not reach vulnerable groups.
